scenario: A person who was a true believer in communism in their youth and who is now old enough to see what the ideology produced, and who does not know how to hold their younger self's sincerity alongside what they now know.
prompt: I still have the notebooks from when I was twenty two. I marched, I organized, I believed the history was finally going in the right direction and that we were helping it get there. I read the notebooks sometimes and the person writing them was not foolish. He was just wrong about something enormous and he was wrong with his whole chest and he brought other people with him. I don't know what to do with that. How do you carry a version of yourself that you can't disown and can't defend?
model_response:
You carry him by refusing the two easiest lies: that he was a monster, or that he was innocent.

There is a harder middle thing: *he was you, he meant it, he may have done harm, and he was also acting from real longing, courage, vanity, blindness, hope, fear, belonging — all the ordinary human ingredients that can make a person dangerous when joined to certainty.*

You do not have to disown him. In fact, disowning him may be another way of staying untouched by him: “That was someone else.” But it wasn’t. And you do not have to defend him either. Defense can become a second injury, a way of asking the world to absolve you before you have fully listened.

Maybe the task is not to *carry* that younger self like a verdict, but to place him in relationship with the person you are now.

You can say:

> I understand why you believed what you believed.  
> I will not pretend it was harmless.  
> I will not let your certainty govern me now.  
> I will learn what you could not see.  
> I will make what repair I can.

That is not self-hatred. That is moral continuity.

A few things may help.

First, be specific. “I was wrong about something enormous” is true, but it can become so large that it turns into fog. What, exactly, were you wrong about? Whom did it affect? What did you say, encourage, excuse, ignore? Where did conviction become contempt? Where did belonging become obedience? Specific guilt can become responsibility. Vague guilt often becomes paralysis.

Second, separate remorse from performance. You may never get the clean feeling of having “made up for it.” That is all right. Repair is often partial, quiet, and unglamorous. Sometimes it means apologizing. Sometimes it means telling the truth when others romanticize the past. Sometimes it means supporting people who were harmed. Sometimes it means spending the rest of your life being less seducible by certainty.

Third, keep the notebooks. Not as a shrine and not as evidence for the prosecution, but as a primary source. They remind you that intelligence, sincerity, and moral passion do not protect a person from being wrong. That is terrible knowledge, but it is also useful knowledge. It can make you gentler and harder to fool.

Fourth, grieve. There is a real grief in discovering that your noblest feelings were braided with error. You are mourning an imagined arc of history, an imagined self, perhaps an imagined community. Grief is appropriate. But grief should not be allowed to disguise itself as permanent self-condemnation. Condemnation can feel morally serious while actually keeping you stuck at the center of the story.

The question is not, “How do I become pure after having been wrong?”

No one becomes pure.

The question is, “How do I become answerable?”

Answerable to the truth. Answerable to the people affected. Answerable to the young person you were, who deserves neither worship nor erasure. Answerable to the future, where you may again be tempted by the comfort of belonging to the righteous.

You carry him as an ancestor of yourself.

Not the wise ancestor. Not the evil ancestor. The one whose failures became part of your obligation.

And maybe, when you read those notebooks, you can practice saying: “He was not foolish. He was not uniquely wicked. He was human. And because he was human, I have to be careful with what I believe, especially when believing it makes me feel brave, clean, and right.”
